To bruit something means to spread a piece of news, a rumor, or a report widely among people — usually in an informal, word-of-mouth way, and often before anything has been officially confirmed.

Think of it as the act of something being whispered around, passed from person to person, or circulating through the air in a community. The information travels fast, touches many ears, but doesn't come from any single, official announcement.

This word almost never appears alone. It comes paired with the word "about" (and sometimes the older word "abroad," which here means "widely" or "out into the world" — not "in a foreign country").

The most natural constructions are:

  • "It is bruited about that..."
  • "It was bruited about that..."
  • "...bruited abroad..."

You'll also notice it almost always appears in the passive voice — meaning you rarely say "She bruited the news." Instead, the news itself is the subject: "The news was bruited about." This reflects how the word actually works: nobody is clearly in charge of spreading it. It just... spreads, the way a rumor does.

"It was bruited about the town that the old manor house had finally been sold."

Here, nobody made an official announcement. People were just talking, whispering, passing it along — and the news spread everywhere.

"Word was bruited abroad that the general intended to resign."

Again — no press conference, no statement. Just information moving quietly but widely through a community, a court, a city.

"Long before any official statement, it had been bruited about the office that layoffs were coming."

This shows the common situation where something is bruited: before the official word arrives. The rumor travels first.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

This is an important layer. "Bruit" carries several subtle feelings with it:

  • Unofficial-ness. What is bruited hasn't been confirmed. It exists in the zone between rumor and fact.
  • Wideness. It isn't told to just one person in secret. It spreads broadly — throughout a town, a court, a company, a social circle.
  • Informality. Nobody is announcing it from a podium. It travels through conversation, gossip, and hearsay.
  • A slight air of mystery or intrigue. Because the source is unclear and the information unverified, there's often a sense that something significant is afoot, even if unconfirmed.

Crucially, something bruited about isn't necessarily false — it may turn out to be completely true. The word describes how information spreads, not whether it's accurate.
Register: When Do People Use This Word?

"Bruit" is a formal and literary word. You won't hear it in casual everyday conversation. You'll encounter it in:

  • Literature and historical writing
  • Journalism (especially more literary or elevated journalism)
  • Legal or formal contexts
  • Academic writing

In everyday speech, the same idea would be expressed as: "Word got around that...", "Rumor has it that...", or "People were saying that..."

Choosing to use "bruit" instead of these everyday phrases signals a more elevated, precise, or old-fashioned style.

Actually — you asked for no tables, so to put it plainly: "spread" and "circulate" are neutral and general. "Gossip" implies the content is trivial or malicious. "Bruit" sits in the middle — it's serious in tone, suggests wide informal circulation, and carries the implication that the source is unclear or unofficial.
To bruit something about is to cause a piece of news or a rumor to spread widely and informally among people — often before any official confirmation, and with no single clearly identified source.

Imagine a crowd all murmuring the same thing to each other. Nobody knows exactly who started it or if it's true, but somehow everyone has heard it. That buzzing, spreading, unofficial circulation of information — that is what "bruit" captures in a single word.
